Winston took a gulp of his black coffee, staring at the notes sprawled across his desk. A murder case at a bungee jumping site was definitely out of the ordinary. Today's victim was a young man named Mack, loud mouthed and cocky by all accounts. 

Mack was bungee jumping the day he was killed. Oddly enough, according to the records, no one else was documented at the bungee jumping site that day, making this case even more peculiar. The first stop for the day was to visit one of Mack's housemates, a woman named Ana. They were seen leaving in the same vehicle from their shared housing complex the morning of the murder, and it was time for Winston to dig deeper. 

As he pulled into the shared housing driveway, a nondescript car came into sight. He learned from neighbours that it was frequently used by multiple residents, but Ana had a peculiar interest in it. She would insist on driving whenever with a group of friends, later meticulously cleaning the car after each use. An idiosyncrasy of hers maybe, but a part of the puzzle nonetheless.

Winston knocked on the door, Ana opened it warily, twiddling a cleaning cloth and spray in her hands and greeted him with a nervous nod. Ana gets nervous and fidgets with the cleaner and cloth when questioned. Winston could sense palpable unease as he started asking her questions.

"Ana, did you not join Mack and the others for bungee jumping today?" Winston questioned, to which she responded, "I signed up to jump. But I didn't end up going through with it."

"Any particular reason you didn't join the others, Ana?" Winston proceeded. 

Ana took a deep breath, "Well sir, my faith doesn't really permit bungee jumping. Truth be told, I was persuaded strongly by Mack. I had even signed up out of peer pressure but couldn't push myself."

It was true – Mack was insisting that everyone in the group should bungee jump. Mack had reportedly also been vocal about ridiculing Ana’s faith, even encouraging others to join him in doing so. It was a significant factor in their relationship.

"Ana, did you and Mack leave in the same car for the bungee jumping event this morning?" Winston gently pushed further.

"Yes. Yes, we did. We always carpool." She responded while anxiously using the cleaner and cloth on her car’s dashboard. Her eyes flickered nervously back to Winston, expecting the next question.

Winston took a deep breath, standing up to leave, "Alright Ana, that should cover everything for now. We'll be in touch."

Ana nervously nodded without looking up from her cleaning, wringing the cloth repeatedly as Winston walked away, left again with another piece to the enigmatic puzzle of Mack's murder.

The day was getting older and Winston was getting more tired, but the case was fresh, and he wasn't one to back down. He tugged on his coat as he approached the bashful teen waiting for him by the police station.

"Mackenzie, it is?" he asked, extending his hand.

"Yeah, that's right." The slight lisp, overlaid with blanket anxiety, confirmed what the school reports suggested.

"You were at the site when Mack... erm... you know," Winston's voice was methodical, calm -- almost robotic. The suspicion on Mackenzie was not unfounded - the security cameras showed him buying nunchaku a week before. 

Mackenzie shifted on his feet, looking away before answering, "Yeah, I was there."

Winston pulled out a small notebook, "What were you doing there, Mackenzie?”

“Bungee jumping, like Mack… Then I left. I didn't... I didn't do anything…” Mackenzie replied.

Internally, Winston sighed at the never-ending waterfall of teenage angst this case was turning into. 

“Martial arts, huh?” Winston segued, gesturing to a bruise on Mackenzie’s knuckles. “Nunchaku particularly, I see? Training does include the use of those, correct?” 

The change in Mackenzie’s demeanor mirrored the bitterness in the last month’s weather – dark eyes replaced with ice-cold ones. “Yeah,” he admitted, shrinking slightly.

Mackenzie always took pride in being the best at everything. So when Mack got everything he wanted - the promotion to team captain, the respect, the attention - it was a hard pill for Mackenzie to swallow. Winston remembered the team talk, Mackenzie was indeed the top candidate but it had gone to Mack instead. 

What clinched it was Mackenzie’s remarks about Mack, echoing whispers of dispute and bickering, lost in the crowded lunchroom. There were also multiple witness reports of the two seen arguing at the bungee jumping site previously. Mackenzie had indeed said disparaging, almost emotional things about Mack – all stemming from a potent brew of jealousy, Winston inferred.

Shifting later through the detritus of Mackenzie's life, Winston discovered the nunchaku that matched the forensics report. They were tucked away, but the layer of dust suggested they weren't a favored possession anymore. It wasn’t hidden, it was misplaced – discarded in the throes of developing maturity.

As the sun started to set, Winston could see witnesses, scattered across the park, repeatedly pointing to the bungee jumping scaffolding. It occurred to him, then, the narrative of the past days. Mackenzie, jealous and wronged, over and over, at the same sight. It was quite a sight. 

Winston, shuffling back to the station, was left with one thought - Looks like Mackenzie had quite an eventful week.

Winston vividly remembered his surprise when he had found nunchaku, a pair of them, while searching Mia's home. Mia had smiled enigmatically, her eyes twinkling with the lethality of secrets untold. "Keep your eyes open, detective," she had replied, her voice a chilling sotto voce lingering between them, hang enough in the suffocating silence.

Winston felt a shiver creep into his spine as he got ready for round two with Mia.

Winston stepped into the dimly lit bowling alley, prowling between lanes like a panther on the hunt. An unusual place to be hammered to death, he thought, especially during the graveyard shift, but a good detective never questioned the chosen venues or the hour of the city's grim reaper. Winston surveyed the empty building, the only sound being that of his own boots echoing off the polished hardwood.

The bartender, one Rosemary – if her nameplate could be trusted – was scrubbing down a countertop at the far corner of the bar. Winston walked over, took a seat on one of the bar stools and introduced himself. 

"I hear you were working here the night Joel was killed," he mentioned, as he watched her movements. 

Rosemary looked up, her face impassive, "Yes, that's true. It was my usual midnight shift, and Joel got murdered after we had closed down for the night. Wasn't much else to do."

"You seem to have keys to this place," Winston noticed, spotting a set of keys on the counter. 

"Yes, I do, for closing hours," she replied, sliding the keys back into her jeans pocket.

He continued his questions, "I understand you practice martial arts, Rosemary?"

For the first time, Rosemary stopped her cleaning and smiled, "Yes, that's right. In fact, I work out regularly at a martial arts gym. Nunchaku workshops are my favorite," she added, her eyes twinkling with something akin to pride.

Winston nodded, imparting no judgement on her preferred pastime. 

Suddenly, a glint at the corner of the room caught his attention. A collection of weaponry displayed on a wall. Upon closer look, he recognized various martial arts weapons, including a pair of nunchaku.

“My father was a big fan of martial arts. He left me his collection," explained Rosemary, noticing his interest. "In fact, the nunchaku you see hanging on the wall is part of my personal collection."

As Winston stood up to leave, he turned to Rosemary, "Did you know Joel well?"

She hesitated for a moment, her eyes downcast, "Joel... he was a good friend. He always wanted to help. And he was the one person who could save me from this terrible debt I'm wrestling with. But to my despair, he... he said no when I asked him for a loan."

Bridget, the ex-wife of Charlie, who was without an evident alibi for the time of the murder. Charlie's life ended tragically in the heart of the swamp, a place where he loved to visit, quite often alone. He was taken down by a lethal crossbow bolt. Winston looked over the notes that had been placed on his desk, details about Jesse, a kid he had been killed by a lawnmower in a rainforest during a school trip. Sighing, he prepared himself to go and speak to Sam, a schoolmate of Jesse with a connection to landscaping tools.

Arriving at "Green Leaves Landscaping", Winston was greeted by the bustling noise of various gardening equipment being operated for demonstrations and repairs. He looked around, noting that this place even had lawnmowers, one in particular stood out.

He was introduced to Sam. The young man, not much older than Jesse, who seemed jittery and nervous. No doubt upset about his friend's death. 

"Sam, right?" Winston asked, to which the young man just nodded. 

"Bit of a strange question, but do you know how to operate a lawnmower?" Winston asked.

A slight nod from Sam confirmed it, "Yeah, on top of that I passed my course in operating heavy machinery with distinction last summer. I know my way around from lawnmowers to bulldozers." 

Winston continued with a gentle but probing conversation, leading to Sam mentioning the school field trip to the rainforest that had turned tragic. This sparked another question from Winston. 

"Anyone else in that rainforest, apart from your school group?" The answer was negative.

The conversation took a dramatic turn when Sam admitted to finding some inappropriate texts between Jesse and his girlfriend on her phone, showing them to Winston. 

"And she admitted to it?" Winston pursued, brows furrowed. "Yes, she confessed when confronted." Sam's voice choked up a little.

Taking a mental step back, Winston continued with his questions, "Your father owns this place?" 

Sam's hand gestured around the landscape store run by his father, "Yeah, been helping him around whenever I'm free."

They chatted for a couple more minutes before Winston thanked Sam for his time and left, informing him that they might need to speak again. He reflected on what he'd learned, about Jesse's cheating, Sam’s landscaping connection and distinction-honored ability to operate heavy machinery. The facts were taking shape in a complex web, beginning to form a picture but with still much to be discovered.

Winston adjusted his fedora and walked into Steve's study in the local synagogue, filled with ancient religious texts, some open and spread out in front of Steve. Steve looked like a man deep in thought, his eyes fixated on the book in front of him. 

"Mind if I interrupt, Rabbi Steve?" Winston asked, interrupting the tranquility. 

"Detective Winston," Steve acknowledged without lifting his eyes. His voice reflected his years, a baritone stained with wisdom. 

"I understand you were meant to be at a number of religious events, which this community is known for, but it appears you were missing in action?" Winston probed lightly, trying to placate the simmering tension he could already sense. 

"I've been studying, Detective. These ancient religious texts are complicated and require my full attention, and I couldn't divide it between them and the ritualistic gatherings." Steve finally looked up, his gaze piercing through Winston.

Steve's intense lifestyle of a lot of reading and self-study was no secret to the detective. This was his daily routine.

"I understand." Winston pulled out his notepad, shifting in his seat. "You regularly volunteer for the forest clean-ups, correct?" 

"Every chance I get," Steve responded, his volunteer spirit evident in his voice. The rain forest thundered just beyond the confines of Steve's synagogue, a song of life against the urban creep. A song that often played the backdrop for Steve's volunteer efforts.

"Yes, I recall there was a cleanup event scheduled for the exact time of Jesse's murder," Winston commented, but left the sentence hanging.

A palpable silence filled the room.

Switching topics, Winston began to inquire about their rival businesses, "Seems like things are going pretty well for Jesse and his lawn care business, while yours seems to be losing steam. In fact, it seems like Jesse planned to undercut your business."

Steve's face twitched slightly at the mention of Jesse. "It's a free market, Detective."

"It is," Winston nodded, "Jesse seems to be gaining a lot of new clients recently." Steve's expression remained unfazed "Quite rapidly, actually. And at the same time, you're losing a bunch of yours.”

"Coincidence," Steve shrugged it off.

"Is it? Or do you suspect Jessie was intentionally stealing your client base?" Winston asked, knowing that Jesse undercutting his rival's price wasn't helping Steve a great deal.

"Talk to the forest, Detective," Steve sighed. “I have more pressing matters to attend to,” Steve said finishing the conversation. 

As Winston got up to leave, he asked off-handedly, "Was the synagogue typically open during those religious events?"

"Yes," Steve confirmed. "It was open to all."

"Thank you for your time, Rabbi Steve," Winston offered a curt nod and left Steve to his ancient texts requiring deep concentration, and shadows while the rainforest sang beyond.

Detective Winston sat busily in his office, perusing online photos of mountain climbing adventures typical of suspect Wade. Eyeing the images, it became immediately apparent among the ropes, carabiners, and pitons that Wade always had one particular piece of gear with him - an axe. Along with the axe, a curious detail drew his attention - a blue bead bracelet that Wade wore on every climb.

As Winston was engrossed in his photographic search, his assistant entered the room, her eyes teary. "Detective, I confronted Wade about my bracelet, the one he keeps wearing," she said, noticeably upset. "He brushed me off, claiming that it became a necessary memento from an infamous climbing adventure with him." 

Scratchy phone recorded deductions hung in the air as a woman's voice filled the room, "Hugo was said to have checked into the campground... the same day as Wade."

Winston tapped the ash from his cigarette into an old coffee mug and decided it was time to have a little chat with Mr. Wade. 

Pulling up to the nearby climbing spot, which was also a well-known campground, he found Wade wiping the sweat off his brow as he examined a climbing route, axe handle sticking out from his backpack. The seasoned detective noted that they were at the plot adjacent to where Hugo had camped.

Wade looked up, seeing Winston step out of his car. "Hey, detective... what brings you out here?"

Winston crossed his arms, gaze lingering on the axe handle. "Thought it was time we had a chat."

Wade chuckled, adjusting the strap of the blue bead bracelet that was hanging loosely on his wrist, "Alright then, shoot."

Winston observed the bracelet, recognizing it from the pictures. Wade had worn the same bracelet during many of his climbs since their unfortunate expedition, even calling it his “lucky charm.” So much so, that it garnered attention on social media.

"My understanding is you venture here quite often for your climbing escapades," Winston inquired.

"That's right," Wade answered casually, seemingly unaware of the implications of Winston’s words.

"And these climbs you embark on... they always need an axe, I presume?" Winston pointed at the tool that held such relevance.

“Depends on the route, detective. Good to have it with me though,” Wade replied, clearly more interested in his climbing equipment than the conversation.

Noting the piece of jewelry, Winston decided the conversation had run its course. "You were camping here the same day as Hugo, weren’t you?"

“Yeah,” Wade replied, losing his grin, “I believe so. We were actually just a few plots apart. Didn’t know him well though.”

“Hmm, alright…” Winston muttered, tipping his hat in goodbye as he got back into his car. His assistant’s bracelet glinted in the sunlight as Wade prepared for his climb. One step in the investigation was over, but many were still left to climb.

Winston was sitting alone in his office, pouring over the sparse details he had on Hugo's murder. The crime scene, a picturesque campground, had been a haven for families just hours before. Winston rubbed his temples, knowing full well that these types of cases took delicate maneuvering, careful data collection. His lead suspect, a man named Salvador, was Hugo's driving instructor. This connection alone might not mean much, but it was a start. 

Winston took a deep breath, called up the local police and made an appointment to subtly interview Salvador. 

Winston found him at the driving school, hands deftly managing a hairpin turn while teaching a student. After the driving lesson ended, Winston introduced himself. 

"Salvador?" 

"Yeah, that's me," he replied, wiping sweat from his brow.

Winston motioned to a nearby bench. "Do you mind if we chat for a few moments?"

Salvador glanced at his watch. "Sure, I've got a few minutes."

They sat. 

"Nice day out, isn't it?" Canvasing the area, Winston's eyes landed on a small poster. The image was of a verdant campground, similar to the one where Hugo was killed. "You like camping, Salvador?"

Salvador, caught off guard, blinked. "Yes, I do. I go regularly, whenever I can... even to that campground over there". 

They chatted about the great outdoors, the joy of being connected with nature, and the complexities of their camping hobbies. Salvador didn’t seem aware that Winston’s questions were leading to anything in particular.

After a few minutes of casual conversation, Winston stood up from the bench. "Thanks for talking with me, Salvador. Nice day, isn't it?" 

"Yes, indeed," Salvador replied, stretching his arms. He watched Winston drove away curiously, before shaking his head and walking back to his car.

Winston's next stop was Salvador's house; he observed from a safe distance as Salvador fiddled with something in his garage. Later, when Salvador had retreated into his house, Winston took a closer look under the cover of darkness. He could see an array of axes, various sizes and shapes, displayed proudly on a wall. He saw newly chopped wood stacked neatly in the corner of his backyard, evidence of Salvador’s recent chopping endeavours.

Winston shared his observations with the local police but stepped back after providing his input. They would carry out any necessary searches with legal authorisations while Winston handled the interviews, suspicions and evidence collecting. It was a symbiotic relationship of professional respect.

The puzzling thing nagging at Winston's mind was Hugo's recent decision to stop supplying Salvador with drugs. Something provoked him to cut off Salvador, who was heavily addicted and relied on those supplies. His need was increasing, the gaps between his fixes shortening. Salvador owed Hugo a considerable sum, standing out amidst all the other jumbled pieces. 

Whenever Winston asked him about the night of the murder, Salvador always shrugged, a feeble excuse always at the ready, nothing concrete or credible. He didn’t provide any strong alibi for where he was that night. He admitted that he was in the vicinity, at that campground where he regularly camped, but no one witnessed him there. It was clear that Salvador knew how to handle an axe, and there was one found at his place that matched the murder weapon.

Winston knew convictions weren't made on this sort of circumstantial evidence, but there were threads that linked Salvador to the crime scene. There was more groundwork to be done. One thing was certain; Winston wouldn’t stop until justice was served.

"She headed towards the swamp... after the concert, going towards the place she loved." The innocent statement caught Winston by surprise. He had stumbled upon someone who had noticed Jess, after Leona's performance, walk blissfully towards the swamp, clutching her VIP pass – the scene of her untimely death.

As Detective Winston thanked Leona for her time, he looked back at the singer, her recently purchased sai cradled in her forearm skillfully as if it were an extension of her own body. Winston couldn't quite shake off the strange sensation that washed over him. Returning to the stillness of his own vehicle, not yet ready to move on, he just sat there under the starlight, trying to make sense of the eerie dance between the facts that were slowly crafting the narrative to this murder. The story had many more veiled layers waiting to be discovered — and some heavy curtains waiting to be lifted.

He peered at the open spot in the case shaping a sai- the exact style like the weapon found in Jess and seemingly missing from the collection. He remembered the local authorities report about a matching weapon disappearing recently. 

Shifting his focus back on Freya, Winston decided to delve deeper. "And you frequent the local dojo, am I correct?" 

"Yes," Freya piped, curious. "I was there just last week."

"And Jess," Winston moved on. "You seem to have spent quite a sum to gain some insight on her."

Flustered, Freya breathed heavily, "Yes, I hired a private investigator. Jess started playing games, bragging about dirt she claimed to have on me."

"How does bird-watching tie into these games?" Winston questioned, casually dropping a seemingly unrelated question.

Taken aback, Freya chuckled awkwardly, "Well detective, I do frequent the swamp near here to observe the local birdlife. And yes, my car was indeed spotted parked there recently."

Seizing the moment, Winston probed, "So you would be quite familiar with navigating the swamplands then?" 

Freya gritted her teeth, "Yes, Detective. As I said, I often go there. My father taught me how to navigate those swamps."

It spoke volumes more than her carefully composed words, "Jess threw accusations left and right, yes. I asked our mutual friends to intervene, to convince her against disclosing these…misconceptions. But, you see, I also heard something disturbing about her. A woman fitting my description was seen heading towards the swamps.” Freya finished, eyes shimmering with unexpected tears.

Winston took a moment to consider her words, nodding slowly, "You've been very helpful, Freya. Thank you." His mind still picking on the revelations, the omissions, the twitches, keeping him aware that the game's just begun.
